name: Wappo
confidence_why: Radin 1929 and Thompson, Park & Li 2006 both place main stress on the first syllable of the stem (the first syllable that is not a prefix), where it stays under suffixation, and Radin's own examples show penult and pre-antepenult stress beside antepenult, so 'antepenult' is only his rough distributional summary and the strict positional count survives only in Gordon 2002's survey coding.
catalog_quote: Accent, exclusively that of stress, is very strong and associated with a definite syllable in each word. In disyllabic words it is always on the first syllable and in polysyllabic words it is practically always on the antepenult. It can be stated, as a general rule, that the vowel accented is the stem vowel and that it rarely shifts no matter how many suffixes are added.

audit.recode_to: morphological (primary stress on the first syllable of the root/stem: prefixes unstressed, suffixes do not shift it; Thompson, Park & Li 2006:1; Radin 1929:12). If a positional label must be kept, at most fixed-dominant, not fixed-strict.
audit.reasoning: The record codes Wappo as fixed-strict antepenult (antepenultimate stress) on the strength of one clause of Radin 1929:12 ('practically always on the antepenult'), inherited from the StressTyp/Gordon 2002 coding; quote/cite/grade fields are empty and the quotation lives only in the domain quotation/the domain locator. (1) Quote: confirmed verbatim at p.12 section 6 in the open UC Berkeley scan downloaded now. (2) But the same paragraph gives the actual rule as stem-vowel stress that does not move under suffixation, and Radin's own examples on that page show penult and pre-antepenult stresses; 'practically always' is itself a hedge incompatible with 'strict'. (3) The modern reference grammar we already hold, Thompson, Park & Li 2006:1, states stress falls on the first non-prefix ('core') syllable, i.e. root-initial, left-anchored to morphology, not counted from the right word edge. Two independent grammars therefore agree

sources.citation: Radin, Paul. 1929. A Grammar of the Wappo Language. University of California Publications in American Archaeology and Ethnology 27. Berkeley: University of California Press. viii+194 pp.
sources.quote: Quote confirmed verbatim. Read in full, section 6 states the rule as stem-vowel stress ('the vowel accented is the stem vowel and ... it rarely shifts no matter how many suffixes are added'), with 'practically always on the antepenult' as a distributional remark. Radin's own illustrations on p.12 are not antepenult: omiso'm-ci 'it becomes evening' (stem som; penult), omoti'se 'it overflows' (stem ti; penult), oko'heleksi 'he is constipated' (stem kohe; pre-antepenult), beside at'a'tasa (antepenult); plus 'in a few futures the accent is shifted' and 'occasionally ... the last vowel of the stem
